title: OCI, Citizenship and Renunciation: What Actually Changes When You Take a Foreign Passport
subtitle: Indian law does not allow dual citizenship. The moment an Indian citizen takes up another country's citizenship, a specific legal consequence follows, and an OCI card is a long-term visa, not a second citizenship, however it may feel in practice.
meta_description: What happens under Indian law when a citizen takes foreign citizenship: Section 9(1), passport surrender, and OCI limits on land, voting and banking.
author: Bhaskar Subramanian, Souvik Bose
author_role: Partner, S&S Co. Advocates & Solicitors; Associate, S&S Co. Advocates & Solicitors
standfirst: Every year, large numbers of Indian citizens become citizens of the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and other countries, and almost all of them later apply for an Overseas Citizen of India card. The two steps feel connected, and in practice they usually happen close together, but they rest on entirely different legal foundations. One is about what Indian law does automatically once a person takes foreign citizenship. The other is a discretionary status the Indian government grants, which can be refused, conditioned or in rare cases cancelled, and which gives real but limited rights, not a second citizenship by another name. This piece sets out what happens at each stage, what an OCI card actually allows and does not allow, and where a recent ruling has pushed the boundary of OCI rights further than many assumed.
key_points: Section 9(1) of the Citizenship Act, 1955 provides that an Indian citizen who voluntarily acquires the citizenship of another country ceases to be an Indian citizen, in substance from the date that foreign citizenship is acquired, not from any later date on which the Indian government gets around to recording it.

That cessation is not left to the individual's own say-so. Courts have held that the actual determination of when citizenship ended, for official purposes, is made by the Central Government under Section 9(2) read with Rule 30 of the Citizenship Rules, 1956, applying statutory rules of evidence, and that a foreign government issuing a passport does not by itself settle that determination.

Holding onto an Indian passport, or continuing to use one, after acquiring foreign citizenship is an offence under the Passports Act, 1967, and Indian missions abroad require a former citizen to obtain both a renunciation certificate and a surrender certificate for the Indian passport, with different requirements depending on whether the foreign citizenship was acquired before or after 1 June 2010.

The Overseas Citizen of India scheme, now governed by Sections 7A to 7D of the Citizenship Act and the Citizenship (Amendment) Rules, is not dual citizenship. It is a long-term, multiple-entry status that gives most of the economic, financial and educational rights of an NRI without conferring voting rights, eligibility for constitutional or government office, or the right to buy agricultural land.

OCI cardholders can buy residential and commercial property in India on broadly the same footing as NRIs, but cannot purchase agricultural land, a farmhouse or plantation property; they can still inherit such property from a resident Indian, though selling inherited agricultural land generally requires transferring it to a resident Indian buyer.

A 2026 Bombay High Court ruling held that an OCI cardholder parent can invoke the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 despite not being an Indian citizen, taking a more generous view than an earlier Karnataka High Court decision on the same question.

Bank accounts held while an Indian citizen generally need to be converted to NRO, NRE or FCNR accounts once residency and citizenship status change; an ordinary resident savings account is not meant to be operated once the holder is no longer resident in India in the sense the banking rules require.

Deciding whether to formally renounce Indian citizenship and move to OCI status, as opposed to simply allowing Section 9(1) to take its course without ever formally renouncing, is less a matter of choice than of timeline and paperwork; the practical difference mainly shows up in the renunciation certificate and in how smoothly the later OCI application proceeds.

sections.heading: The one rule everything else in this piece follows from
paragraphs: Section 9(1) of the Citizenship Act, 1955 states the position plainly: an Indian citizen who voluntarily acquires the citizenship of another country ceases, from that point, to be a citizen of India. India does not recognise dual citizenship for its own nationals, unlike some other countries that permit their citizens to hold a second passport without losing the first. The moment a person completes the process of becoming, say, a US, Canadian, British or Australian citizen, by naturalisation, registration or any other voluntary act of acquiring that citizenship, Indian citizenship ends as a matter of law.

The word voluntarily matters here. A child who acquires a foreign citizenship automatically at birth because a parent held that citizenship, without any voluntary act of the child's own, is not caught by Section 9(1) in the same way, and the position of such dual-citizen-by-birth children, until they are old enough to make their own voluntary choices about citizenship, has generated its own body of separate commentary and case law that this piece does not attempt to cover. The focus here is the far more common case: an adult Indian citizen who moves abroad, settles, and after some years voluntarily applies for and receives the citizenship of the country where they have been living.

This also distinguishes citizenship acquired voluntarily from a status such as permanent residency, a green card in the American system, residency in Canada short of citizenship, or indefinite leave to remain in the UK. None of these intermediate statuses amounts to acquiring a foreign citizenship for the purposes of Section 9(1), so a person who holds a green card or similar status but has not yet naturalised as a citizen of that other country remains an Indian citizen throughout, continues to hold and use an Indian passport without any of the issues discussed below, and only reaches the point this piece is concerned with once the formal step of naturalisation, or its equivalent in the relevant country, is actually completed.

sections.heading: What 'automatic' actually means in practice
paragraphs: It is tempting to read Section 9(1) as meaning Indian citizenship simply evaporates the instant a foreign citizenship certificate is issued, with no further step required. That is broadly correct as a statement of substantive law, but Indian courts have been careful to separate the legal fact of cessation from its official determination. Section 9(2) of the Act, read with Rule 30 of the Citizenship Rules, 1956, gives the Central Government the power to decide, in case of doubt, whether and when a person's citizenship terminated, and that determination is made on the authority's own assessment of the evidence, not simply accepted from whatever the foreign country's passport or citizenship certificate says.

Courts have specifically rejected the idea that a foreign government's act of issuing a passport to a former Indian citizen automatically and conclusively proves, for every purpose under Indian law, exactly when that person's Indian citizenship ended. The authority under Section 9(2) decides this question applying its own statutory rules of evidence. In the great majority of ordinary cases this distinction does not create any real difficulty, since the date of naturalisation is clear and undisputed, but it matters in contested cases, for instance where a person's citizenship status is disputed in a property, inheritance or criminal matter years after the fact, and where the precise date citizenship ended turns out to carry legal consequences the person did not anticipate at the time.

sections.heading: Surrendering the passport: renunciation certificate, surrender certificate, and the 2010 cutoff
paragraphs: Because Indian law does not recognise the dual status, a person who has acquired foreign citizenship is required to formally deal with their Indian passport rather than simply let it lapse on its own expiry date. Indian missions abroad describe this as a two-stage process: first, a renunciation of Indian citizenship is formally accepted by the competent authority and a renunciation certificate issued, and second, once that is done, the person surrenders the physical Indian passport itself and receives a surrender certificate confirming that the passport has been cancelled and surrendered.

The date on which foreign citizenship was acquired affects both the fee charged for this process and, in the view taken by some missions, the strictness of the requirement itself. Missions commonly draw the line at 1 June 2010: a person who acquired foreign citizenship on or after that date is expected to go through the full renunciation and surrender process as described, while a person whose foreign citizenship predates that cutoff, and whose Indian passport was already cancelled by the Indian consulate at the time, may not need a fresh surrender certificate for a passport that no longer exists in usable form. The specific mission's current requirements and fee schedule should be checked directly, since practice and fees vary somewhat between missions and are liable to change.

Applications for renunciation and surrender are generally made online through the government's passport portal, supported by documents including the original Indian passport, a copy of the foreign citizenship certificate, and, where applicable, an affidavit explaining any gap between acquiring foreign citizenship and applying for renunciation, particularly where the Indian passport was retained or used for travel during that gap. That affidavit requirement exists because continuing to hold, renew, or travel on an Indian passport after acquiring foreign citizenship is treated seriously under Indian law and is not simply an administrative oversight to be waved through.

sections.heading: The offence most people do not realise they are committing
paragraphs: Section 9(1) ending Indian citizenship does not, by itself, stop a person from physically holding an Indian passport if they simply never tell anyone about their new foreign citizenship. That gap between the legal fact and the practical document is precisely what the Passports Act, 1967 is designed to close. Applying for an Indian passport, continuing to hold one, getting one renewed or reissued, or travelling on one after acquiring foreign citizenship is a punishable offence under that Act, and this is not a theoretical risk: Indian missions and passport authorities actively check for exactly this pattern when a renunciation or fresh passport application is filed, which is why the affidavit mentioned above is required wherever there has been a delay.

The practical message for anyone who has recently taken foreign citizenship, or is in the process of doing so, is straightforward: the time to start the renunciation and surrender process is as soon as the foreign citizenship is granted, not whenever it becomes convenient. Continuing to use the Indian passport for travel in the meantime, even for what feels like a single necessary trip, is the specific conduct the law treats as an offence, and it is also the detail most likely to complicate an otherwise routine renunciation application later.

sections.heading: From citizen to OCI: what the scheme actually is
paragraphs: Once Indian citizenship has ended, the great majority of former citizens apply for Overseas Citizen of India status, commonly described using the older but still widely used shorthand of an OCI card. The scheme is governed by Sections 7A to 7D of the Citizenship Act, 1955, inserted by amendment, and its substantive content, meaning exactly what an OCI cardholder can and cannot do, is set by the Central Government through notification under Section 7B(1) rather than fixed permanently in the statute itself. The current framework rests on a notification issued in March 2021, which replaced three earlier notifications dating back to 2005, 2007 and 2009, and because the rights are set this way, by executive notification rather than primary legislation, they can and have changed over time, which is worth keeping in mind rather than assuming today's position is permanent.

The name is, in one respect, misleading. An OCI card is not citizenship of India in any constitutional sense, and the government and courts have both been consistent that it should not be described or relied upon as dual citizenship. It is better understood as a long-term, multiple-entry immigration and civil-rights status, a lifelong visa combined with a defined, government-set bundle of economic and civil entitlements that approximate, but do not duplicate, the position of a resident Indian citizen.

History matters a little here, because the scheme as it exists now also absorbed an older, separate status. India used to run a distinct Person of Indian Origin, or PIO, card scheme alongside OCI, with its own, somewhat different set of benefits. The 2015 amendment to the Citizenship Act merged that separate PIO scheme into OCI, deeming existing PIO cardholders to be OCI cardholders from that point and stopping the issue of any further PIO cards. A person still travelling on an old, undocumented PIO card today should treat it as a legacy document rather than assume it continues to carry exactly the same practical standing as a current OCI card, and is generally better served by obtaining the actual OCI card reflecting that deemed status rather than relying on the older PIO card at an airport or government office years after the scheme closed.

sections.heading: What an OCI card actually gives you
paragraphs: Set that aside, though, and the central practical benefit is a multiple-entry, lifelong visa to visit India for any purpose, removing the need to apply for a fresh visa before each trip, which is the feature most former citizens value most immediately. Beyond travel, the 2021 notification gives OCI cardholders parity with non-resident Indians across most economic, financial and educational matters: the ability to invest, to open and hold NRI-type bank accounts, to pursue most forms of higher education on the same basis as an NRI applicant, and to take up employment in the private sector without a separate work visa or registration requirement, subject to the general exceptions described below.

OCI cardholders are also generally exempted from the registration requirements that would otherwise apply to a foreign national on a long stay in India, and are treated as NRIs rather than as foreign nationals for most day-to-day civil and commercial purposes, a distinction that matters for everything from opening a bank account to buying non-agricultural property.

sections.heading: What an OCI card does not give you
paragraphs: Section 7B(2) of the Citizenship Act sets out a specific list of rights an OCI cardholder does not get, and the list is worth knowing precisely rather than assuming it tracks ordinary intuition about what a long-term resident might expect. An OCI cardholder cannot vote in any Indian election, cannot be elected or appointed to any of the constitutional offices the provision names, among them the offices of President, Vice-President, and judge of the Supreme Court or a High Court, and cannot hold any government post except where the Central Government specifically permits appointment to a particular service or post by special order. These exclusions exist because OCI status is, deliberately, not citizenship, and the political and sovereign functions of the state remain reserved for citizens alone.

The other significant restriction concerns land. An OCI cardholder cannot purchase agricultural land, a farmhouse, or plantation property in India, a restriction that sits in the Foreign Exchange Management Act framework and the Non-Debt Instruments Rules, 2019 rather than in the Citizenship Act itself, but that operates as a practical limit on OCI status all the same. OCI cardholders can buy other immovable property, residential or commercial, broadly as an NRI can, and this is the restriction examined in more detail in the next section because it is the one that catches out the most people in practice.

A further, narrower restriction concerns travel to areas the government designates as protected or restricted, typically for security reasons in border or sensitive regions, where an OCI cardholder, like other foreign nationals, generally needs specific permission before travelling, a requirement that an ordinary Indian citizen does not face.

Employment deserves a slightly closer look, because the general parity OCI cardholders enjoy in the private sector does not extend to every kind of work. Beyond the outright bar on ordinary government service except by special order, certain professions and roles that are reserved for citizens under separate statutes or regulatory frameworks, including some regulated professions and specific categories of research or strategic work, remain closed to an OCI cardholder in the same way they would be closed to any other foreign national, regardless of how long that person has held OCI status or how settled their life in India has become. Anyone taking up a specific regulated role, rather than ordinary private-sector employment, should check the governing statute or regulator's own rules on citizenship rather than assume the general OCI employment parity extends automatically to that particular field.

sections.heading: Agricultural land, inheritance, and the sale of land you did not buy
paragraphs: The bar on purchasing agricultural land, a farmhouse or plantation property applies regardless of how long someone has held OCI status or how settled their life in India has otherwise become, and it is not a matter of needing special permission to buy such land; the position commonly described by Indian missions and by commercial guidance is a straightforward prohibition on purchase, not a permission route subject to approval. An older framing, sometimes still repeated, describes this as requiring Reserve Bank of India permission rather than being an outright bar, and the more recent and more consistently reported position is the flat prohibition rather than an approval mechanism, so anyone relying on an older source on this point should treat it with caution and confirm the current position before acting.

Inheritance is the significant exception. An OCI cardholder, like an NRI, can inherit agricultural land, a farmhouse or plantation property from a person who was resident in India at the time of the relevant transfer, whether under a will or under the ordinary rules of intestate succession. What an OCI cardholder generally cannot do is then sell that inherited land to another OCI cardholder, an NRI, or a foreign national; the usual position is that such land can only be sold to a person resident in India, and transferring or selling inherited agricultural or plantation land in some cases needs separate approval, which is a point worth confirming with the specific bank or authority involved before any sale is agreed, since the position on approval requirements has not been entirely consistent across sources.

A gift of agricultural land to an OCI cardholder follows a similarly narrow route: such a gift is generally permitted only from a person resident in India, not from another OCI cardholder or NRI, which closes off an obvious workaround some families might otherwise consider, where land is passed between two non-resident family members through a gift rather than a sale.

Families sometimes try a different workaround instead, buying agricultural land in the name of a resident relative, such as a sibling who stayed in India, with the understanding that the OCI family member is the real beneficial owner behind the arrangement. This kind of informal arrangement raises its own serious legal risk under the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988, which generally prohibits exactly this pattern, a transaction held in another person's name for the real benefit of someone who could not have held it directly, and can expose both the nominal owner and the real beneficiary to confiscation of the property and separate penal consequences. Using a resident relative as a nominee to get around the agricultural land restriction is not a safe planning technique, whatever the family's intentions, and should not be treated as a practical shortcut around a rule that exists for a reason.

sections.heading: Banking: what changes once citizenship and residency both change
paragraphs: Banking is where this shows up most routinely. A resident savings account held while a person was still an Indian citizen and resident is not meant to continue operating in the same form once that person becomes a non-resident, whether as an NRI or as an OCI cardholder. The ordinary expectation under the foreign exchange framework is that such accounts are converted to Non-Resident Ordinary (NRO) status, or that funds are moved into a Non-Resident External (NRE) or Foreign Currency Non-Resident (FCNR) account depending on the source and currency of the funds involved, and continuing to operate an unconverted resident account after becoming non-resident is not consistent with the rules governing those accounts.

OCI cardholders are treated the same way NRIs are for the purpose of opening and operating these account types, which is a convenience in one sense, since the process and the bank's own forms do not usually distinguish sharply between an NRI and an OCI applicant, but it also means an OCI cardholder faces the same restrictions an NRI does on using a domestic resident account for ordinary banking once residency has changed. This piece does not go into the detailed tax treatment of interest on these accounts, repatriation limits, or the separate questions around EPF, PPF and pension accounts on leaving India, each of which raises its own distinct set of rules beyond the scope of what is covered here.

sections.heading: The Bombay High Court's 2026 ruling on OCI cardholders and the Senior Citizens Act
paragraphs: A notable recent development shows how courts are willing to read welfare-oriented statutes generously in favour of OCI cardholders even where the statute itself does not mention OCI status at all. In Mughda Sahal v. Senior Citizen Appellate Tribunal and Another, decided on 11 June 2026, the Bombay High Court held that an OCI cardholder parent could invoke the protections of the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007, despite no longer holding Indian citizenship, reasoning that the object of that Act, protecting the welfare of elderly parents, was better served by an approach that leaned in favour of extending its protection rather than reading citizenship as a strict precondition the Act itself does not actually impose. The court allowed the writ petition, set aside the Appellate Tribunal's order, and restored the Maintenance Tribunal's earlier order in the cardholder's favour.

The Bombay High Court was explicit that it was departing from a narrower view the Karnataka High Court had taken on the same question in Dephny Gladys Lobo, finding that the earlier decision had not adequately considered either the Senior Citizens Act's underlying purpose or the Citizenship Act framework and the 2021 OCI notification. This leaves the two High Courts in open disagreement on the point, which means an OCI cardholder parent's ability to rely on the Senior Citizens Act may currently depend on which state the matter arises in, at least until the Supreme Court or a larger bench resolves the conflict, and anyone relying on the Mughda Sahal position outside Maharashtra should check the current state of authority in the relevant state before assuming it will be followed.

Looking at the facts, the underlying dispute in Mughda Sahal arose from an eviction order, where the Maintenance Tribunal had initially ruled in the OCI cardholder's favour under the Senior Citizens Act before the Appellate Tribunal reversed that outcome on the citizenship question, which the Bombay High Court then set aside, restoring the original Tribunal order. The case is a useful illustration of a broader pattern worth watching rather than a one-off curiosity: as OCI cardholders age and more of them face exactly this kind of family or property dispute in India, courts are increasingly being asked to decide whether a welfare statute drafted without OCI status in mind should be read to include OCI cardholders, and the answer so far has not been uniform across different courts facing a similar question under similar welfare legislation.

sections.heading: Deciding between formal renunciation and simply letting Section 9(1) take its course
paragraphs: Because Section 9(1) operates as a matter of law once foreign citizenship is voluntarily acquired, a person technically ceases to be an Indian citizen whether or not they ever file a formal renunciation application. In practice, though, treating renunciation as optional rather than as the next required step creates exactly the documentary gap, an uncancelled Indian passport, no renunciation certificate, no clean paper trail, that later complicates an OCI application, a property transaction, or a dispute over when citizenship actually ended. The formal renunciation and surrender process exists precisely to close that gap cleanly and on the record, and there is little practical advantage, and real risk, in delaying it once foreign citizenship has been acquired.

The one genuine choice most people face is not whether to renounce, since that follows automatically from the law once foreign citizenship is taken, but how quickly to deal with the passport and renunciation paperwork, and whether to apply for OCI status immediately afterwards or at some later point. Applying for OCI promptly after completing renunciation tends to produce a smoother process than doing so years later, when supporting documents, name-change records, or even the renunciation certificate itself may need to be tracked down again.

Family members sometimes ask whether it is possible to skip the Indian side of this process entirely and simply let the old Indian passport expire unused, treating the expiry date as a natural, informal end point rather than going through renunciation at all. This does not actually solve anything, since Section 9(1) has already ended Indian citizenship by operation of law regardless of what happens to the passport, and an expired, unsurrendered passport still leaves exactly the documentary gap described above, without even the benefit of a renunciation certificate to show for it. There is no informal shortcut that avoids the formal process while still leaving a clean record for later use, and the small amount of time the formal route takes is a reasonable price for not having to reconstruct that record from scratch years later.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls worth naming directly
paragraphs: Topping the list, the most frequent practical mistake is continuing to use an Indian passport for travel after acquiring foreign citizenship, usually explained afterwards as a simple oversight or a desire to avoid visa paperwork for one more trip, but treated by the Passports Act as the specific offence it is. A second common mistake is assuming that OCI status, once granted, is functionally identical to citizenship for every purpose, which leads some cardholders to be genuinely surprised when told they cannot vote, cannot buy a plot of agricultural land for a retirement farmhouse, or cannot take up certain government-linked roles.

A third pitfall involves inherited agricultural land specifically: a family sometimes assumes that because the OCI cardholder inherited the land lawfully, it can then be transferred freely within the wider family, including to another OCI cardholder or NRI relative, without appreciating that the sale restriction to a resident Indian buyer still applies to that inherited land even though the inheritance itself was unproblematic. None of these pitfalls are especially complicated once named, but each of them shows up repeatedly in practice precisely because the underlying rules are set by notification and FEMA regulation rather than by anything most people read before the fact.

Timing causes a fourth, quieter pitfall around the renunciation and OCI application sequence itself. Some people apply for OCI status before formally completing the renunciation and passport surrender process in the mistaken belief that holding an approved foreign citizenship is enough on its own, only to find the OCI application held up or queried because the Indian authorities expect to see the renunciation certificate as part of a clean, documented sequence from Indian citizen to foreign citizen to OCI cardholder. Keeping the paperwork in the correct order, renunciation and surrender first, OCI application second, avoids this particular delay entirely and is worth treating as a fixed sequence rather than a flexible one.

sections.heading: OCI and the next generation: children born abroad to Indian-origin parents
paragraphs: Succession planning for a mixed-status family raises a separate but related question for children born outside India to parents who are OCI cardholders or who were themselves Indian citizens before naturalising abroad. A child born abroad to a parent who is already an OCI cardholder can generally be registered as an OCI minor in their own right, subject to the eligibility conditions the citizenship rules set for OCI registration generally, including the usual exclusions for countries whose nationals are not eligible for OCI status at all. This matters in practice because families sometimes assume OCI status passes down automatically the way citizenship does in some other countries, when in fact a separate registration application, with its own documents and fees, is needed for each child.

Where a family includes a mix of Indian citizen children, born before a parent naturalised abroad, and foreign citizen children, born after, the two sets of children can end up with materially different rights in India, the citizen children retaining full citizenship rights including the ability to inherit and hold agricultural land without restriction, and the OCI children facing the restrictions described throughout this piece. This is a detail worth working through deliberately in succession planning rather than assumed to be uniform across siblings simply because they share the same parents.

sections.heading: What an OCI card does for inheritance and succession generally
paragraphs: Beyond the specific agricultural land restriction already discussed, an OCI cardholder's position in Indian succession law is broadly the same as that of an NRI, which is to say governed by the same personal law, testamentary or intestate, that would apply to any other heir of the same religion and family background, without any special OCI-specific carve-out beyond the land rules. An OCI cardholder can inherit non-agricultural immovable property, bank balances, shares and other assets from an Indian resident on the same footing as any other heir, and can equally leave such assets to heirs of their own by will, including heirs who are themselves foreign citizens or OCI cardholders.

In practice, the complications that do arise in this area tend to come not from any special OCI restriction but from the ordinary friction of cross-border succession: foreign wills needing probate or at least recognition in India, foreign grants of probate or letters of administration needing to be re-sealed or separately applied for in an Indian court, and banks or land registries sometimes being unfamiliar with how to process a claim from an heir holding a foreign passport and an OCI card rather than an Indian passport. None of this is unique to OCI cardholders as against NRIs more generally, and the practical steps for managing it are the same ones our existing article on succession, wills, probate and repatriation for NRIs already sets out in more detail.

conclusion: The legal position running through all of this is simpler than the paperwork around it suggests. Indian citizenship ends, as a matter of law, the moment another citizenship is voluntarily taken up, and everything else, the passport surrender, the OCI application, the civil rights that follow, is the administrative and practical working-out of that one underlying rule. Getting the sequence right, dealing with the passport promptly, applying for OCI once that is done, and understanding precisely which rights the OCI card carries and which it does not, avoids most of the difficulties that otherwise surface years later in a property dispute, a bank account query or a question about who can act for an elderly parent.

Where the law genuinely remains unsettled, as with the split between the Bombay and Karnataka High Courts on the Senior Citizens Act, or with older commentary on agricultural land that has not kept pace with the current position, treating the uncertainty as real rather than assuming either the most convenient or the most restrictive reading is the safer course until a higher court or a fresh notification settles the point.

Because OCI rights rest on executive notification rather than on a fixed statutory text, this entire area moves more than most areas of civil law, and a position stated confidently today can be modified by a later notification without the Citizenship Act itself changing at all. Checking the current Ministry of Home Affairs notification before relying on any specific entitlement, rather than relying on this piece or any other secondary source indefinitely into the future, remains the sound practice for exactly that reason.

faqs.q: Does my Indian citizenship end automatically the day I become a citizen of another country, or only once the Indian government formally records it?
faqs.a: As a matter of substantive law under Section 9(1) of the Citizenship Act, citizenship ends from the date the foreign citizenship is voluntarily acquired. The Central Government's power under Section 9(2) to determine the question in case of dispute is about resolving uncertainty over that date and the surrounding facts, not about creating some later date on which citizenship actually ends; in practice, though, dealing with the passport and renunciation paperwork promptly avoids the question ever becoming disputed.

faqs.q: What happens if I keep using my Indian passport for a while after getting a foreign passport?
faqs.a: Continuing to hold, renew or travel on an Indian passport after voluntarily acquiring foreign citizenship is an offence under the Passports Act, 1967. It is also the single most common complication in later renunciation applications, since an affidavit explaining the gap and any passport use during that period is typically required.

faqs.q: Is an OCI card the same thing as dual citizenship?
faqs.a: No. India does not permit dual citizenship, and an OCI card is a separate, government-granted status, essentially a lifelong multiple-entry visa with a defined bundle of economic and civil rights, not citizenship under a different name. The distinction matters most clearly around voting, constitutional and government office, and agricultural land, none of which an OCI card confers.

faqs.q: Can I buy a farmhouse or agricultural land in India as an OCI cardholder?
faqs.a: No, not by purchase. OCI cardholders, like NRIs, cannot buy agricultural land, a farmhouse or plantation property under the current Foreign Exchange Management Act framework. Such property can still be acquired by inheritance from a resident Indian, though reselling inherited agricultural land generally requires selling to a resident Indian buyer rather than to another OCI cardholder or NRI.

faqs.q: Can an OCI cardholder vote in Indian elections or hold public office?
faqs.a: No. Section 7B(2) of the Citizenship Act specifically excludes OCI cardholders from voting rights and from election or appointment to constitutional offices, including the offices of President, Vice-President and judge of the Supreme Court or a High Court. Government employment is also generally excluded, except where the Central Government specifically permits appointment to a named service or post.

faqs.q: Can an OCI cardholder claim maintenance from their children under Indian law, or claim protection as a senior citizen?
faqs.a: The Bombay High Court held in June 2026, in Mughda Sahal v. Senior Citizen Appellate Tribunal, that an OCI cardholder parent can invoke the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 despite not holding Indian citizenship. The Karnataka High Court has taken a narrower view on a similar question, so the position may currently differ depending on the state, pending a definitive ruling from a higher court.

faqs.q: What happens to my ordinary Indian savings account once I become an OCI cardholder?
faqs.a: A resident savings account is generally expected to be converted to a Non-Resident Ordinary (NRO) account, with funds in appropriate currencies moved to NRE or FCNR accounts as relevant, once the holder is no longer resident in India in the sense the banking rules require. OCI cardholders are treated the same way NRIs are for opening and operating these non-resident account types.

faqs.q: I acquired foreign citizenship years ago but never formally renounced my Indian citizenship. Is that a problem now?
faqs.a: It can create real practical difficulties, since an unresolved renunciation leaves an evidentiary gap about exactly when Indian citizenship ended and whether the Indian passport was properly surrendered in the meantime. Completing the renunciation and surrender process now, even belatedly, through the relevant Indian mission, is generally far better than leaving the position unresolved indefinitely, and it is the necessary first step before any OCI application can proceed smoothly.

verification_notes: Section 9(1) and the Section 9(2)/Rule 30 determination mechanism are corroborated by multiple independent sources (advocatekhoj's bare act text, a Delhi High Court decision summary on a Singapore-citizenship case, and a Supreme Court excerpt on the evidentiary nature of the Section 9(2) determination), consistent with each other. The 1 June 2010 cutoff and the two-certificate renunciation and surrender process are corroborated across at least three independent Indian mission websites (Hong Kong, Toronto and Birmingham), consistent on the substance though differing slightly in fee figures by mission, so this piece does not state a specific fee figure and directs readers to the specific mission instead. The OCI property restriction on agricultural land, farmhouse and plantation property, and the inheritance exception, are corroborated from multiple independent commercial and legal sources (an official mission benefits page, Khaitan & Co, Whytecroft Ford and Rustomjee) that are consistent with each other on a flat prohibition on purchase; one older Tribune India report from a 2020-era notification period describes this instead as requiring RBI permission, which conflicts with the more recent and more numerous sources, so this piece flags that older framing explicitly as outdated rather than treating it as a live alternative, and it does not state that RBI approval is currently available as a purchase route. Section 7B(2)'s specific exclusions (voting, constitutional office, government employment absent special order) are corroborated from multiple independent sources consistent on substance, though this piece does not attempt to reproduce the full text of every sub-clause verbatim given some inconsistency in how different secondary sources phrase the list. Mughda Sahal v. Senior Citizen Appellate Tribunal (Bombay High Court, decided 11 June 2026) is corroborated from at least three independent sources (LiveLaw, Free Press Journal and Outlook Money), consistent on the case name, decision date, core holding, the disagreement with the Karnataka High Court's Dephny Gladys Lobo decision, and the outcome restoring the Maintenance Tribunal's order; the full text of the judgment itself was not directly retrieved because court-hosted PDF access was blocked by this session's network policy, so the holding is stated at the level of generality the converging secondary reports support, and this is flagged rather than presented as primary verification. The precise current number of states that have adopted the 2021 OCI notification's specific wording, and the exact figure for total OCI cardholders worldwide, were not found in reliable form in this run and are not stated in this piece. The 2015 merger of the PIO card scheme into OCI, and its effective date of 6 January 2015, is corroborated from at least two independent sources (Nishith Desai Associates' hotline note and a Bankbazaar explainer), consistent with each other on the substance of the merger and the deemed conversion of existing PIO holders.
